sentences.text: The name Diluvicursor translates to "flood runner," a title chosen because the fossil was unearthed in a high-energy river setting.
The specific epithet pickeringi commemorates David A. Pickering, a distinguished Australian paleontologist who passed away before the research was finalized.
The primary specimen, known as the holotype, preserves an almost complete articulated tail that lacks only the first, second, and twelfth vertebrae.
Scientists have identified ten unique derived features that distinguish this animal from its relatives.
In the third through sixth tail vertebrae, the spinous processes are notably low, measuring no higher than their front-to-back width.
The holotype individual was an older juvenile estimated to be 1.2 meters long, roughly the size of a modern wild turkey.
Adult members of this species likely reached at least 2.3 meters in length, a size comparable to that of an emu.
This dinosaur is notably larger than the more recent ornithischians discovered at Dinosaur Cove.
Remains of Diluvicursor were found in 2005 within the Eumeralla Formation and were formally named in early 2018.
A partial tail vertebra belonging to a larger individual discovered nearby in the same deposit was also assigned to this taxon.
Diluvicursor was likely a plant-eater that consumed low vegetation such as Pteridophyta, Hepaticae, Lycopsida, Cycadophyta, Bennettitales, and Taeniopteridae.
Researchers hypothesize that the carcass became trapped in plant debris on a tree stump in a deep, high-energy river before being dragged by a current and quickly deposited in thick mud.

The low height of the spinous processes in the third to sixth tail vertebrae indicates a specialized form of movement, and researchers suggest that the widening of muscles likely improved walking ability by allowing the femur to be pushed back with greater force.
Cladistic analysis places Diluvicursor within Cerapoda, and the animal belongs to the class Ornithischia.
The parent group of Diluvicursor is Elasmaria, and phylogenetic analysis recovered it as a basal elasmarian and the sister taxon to Anabisetia.

Descriptives considered the placement of Diluvicursor among Euornithopoda to be tentative, while traditional comparative methods suggest it is related to Anabisetia, Gasparinisaura, the family Dryosauridae, and possibly the Antarctic dinosaur Morrosaurus.
Diluvicursor pickeringi lived approximately 113 million years ago during the Albian stage of the Early Cretaceous in what is now Australia.
More specifically, it inhabited the early Albian stage in Victoria, southeastern Australia, near Cape Otway, between 113.2 and 110.1 million years ago.

It is debated whether Diluvicursor is synonymous with other small-bodied ornithopods from the same formation due to a lack of overlapping anatomical material, and it is also debated whether Diluvicursor is identical to Atlascopcosaurus, though evidence suggests at least two ornithischians were present at the site.
